title: Antimicrobial and biodegradable hydrogel based on nanocellulose/alginate incorporated with silver nanoparticles as active packaging for poultry products.

Materials and methods
Materials
CNFs from coconut husk were prepared according to the CNF isolation method of Hongrattanavichit and Aht-
Ong16, in which coconut husk waste was supplied by a coconut farm at Prachuap Khiri Khan, Thailand. Briefly, 
the coconut husk was separated using a sieve with number 20 mesh (0.841-mm diameter) prior to treatment 
by a chemimechanical process. The chemicals used in the experiments of CNF preparation and CNF hydrogel 
preparation,  including  sodium  hydroxide  pellets,  hydrogen  peroxide,  calcium  chloride,  and  glycerol,  were 
purchased from CT Chemical (Bangkok, Thailand). Silver nanoparticles and sodium alginate were purchased 
from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). All purchased chemicals were of analytical reagent grade.

Scientific Reports |        (2024) 14:27135 

| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-78677-9

2

 www.nature.com/scientificreports/

Preparation of the nanocellulose hydrogel composited with silver nanoparticles (AgH)
AgH was prepared at various concentrations of silver nanoparticles (0, 0.0078, 0.0156, 0.0312, and 0.0624 phr), 
which corresponded to AgH0, AgH0.0078, AgH0.0156, AgH0.0312, and AgH0.0624, respectively. Eight parts of 
0.50% w/v CNF were mixed with two parts of 0.25% w/v sodium alginate and 5-phr glycerol for 20 min under 
continuous stirring. Then, the different concentrations of silver nanoparticles were added to the solution. The 
mixture was then stirred until the solution was homogeneous and ultrasonicated to eliminate tiny bubbles. The 
mixed solution was placed into a polypropylene mold and aged for 24 h. Finally, 2 M calcium chloride was used 
to transform the solution into a hydrogel using a crosslinking mechanism. The CNF hydrogel was immersed in 
deionized (DI) water to make the exchange between calcium chloride and DI water.

Characterization of the CNF hydrogel
Morphological properties
The cross-sectional morphology and composition of the silver nanoparticles in the CNF hydrogel composites 
at various silver nanoparticle concentrations were observed using field-emission scanning electron microscopy 
(FESEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (JSM-7610 F, JEOL, Tokyo, Japan). Prior to observation, 
all hydrogel samples were solvent exchanged in absolute ethanol and dehydrated using the supercritical drying 
method. Then, the samples were coated with gold to prevent static electric charging. Finally, each sample was 
monitored at an acceleration voltage of 5.0 kV with a magnification of 20,000×.

Crystallinity
The  crystallinity  indices  of  the  CNF  hydrogel  composites  at  various  silver  nanoparticle  concentrations  were 
measured using an X-ray diffractometer (D8 ADVANCE, Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA). Prior to measurement, 
all  hydrogel  samples  were  solvent  exchanged  in  absolute  ethanol  and  dehydrated  using  the  supercritical 
drying method. The XRD program was set to detect the angle of 2θ in the range of 5°–40°. The percentage of 
crystallinityindex (Icr) was calculated from Eq. (1), according to Segal, et al.17.

Icr (%) = [(I002 −

Iam) /I002]

100 

×

(1)

 where I002 is the maximum intensity of the lattice diffraction peak at 2θ around 21°–23°, which is attributed to 
the Iβ crystalline phase, and Iam is the minimum intensity of the amorphous region at 2θ around 16°–18°, which 
is attributed to the amorphous phase.

Thermal properties
The  thermal  stability  of  the  CNF  hydrogel  composites  at  various  silver  nanoparticle  concentrations  was 
evaluated using TGA (TGA/DSC 3 + STARe System, Mettler Toledo, Columbus, OH, USA). Prior to evaluation, 
all hydrogel samples were solvent exchanged in absolute ethanol and dehydrated using the supercritical drying 
method. The heating rate and temperature range of the test were set at 10 ℃/min and 50–600 ℃, respectively. 
All samples were characterized under nitrogen atmosphere with a N2 flow rate of 30 ml/min.

Mechanical properties
The mechanical properties in terms of shear testing of the CNF hydrogel composites at various silver nanoparticle 
concentrations were determined using a rheometer (HAAKE MARS 40, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany). 
The  rheological  testing  program  was  operated  at  a  20-mm  parallel-plate  configuration  and  a  gap  distance  of 
approximately 2 mm. Prior to testing, the sample was placed at the center of the base plate, which controlled the 
temperature and the heating and cooling rates at 25 ℃ and 1 ℃/min, respectively. A strain sweep in oscillatory 
mode was conducted from 0.001 to 10.000% log at a fixed frequency rate of 1.000 Hz. The storage modulus (G′) 
and loss modulus (G″) were recorded during testing.

Antimicrobial properties

evaluated using a testing method adapted from the AATCC 100–2004 standard. E. coli and S. aureus, which 
were  assigned  to  Gram-negative  bacteria  and  Gram-positive  bacteria,  respectively,  were  selected  to  evaluate

meta.title: Antimicrobial and biodegradable hydrogel based on nanocellulose/alginate incorporated with silver nanoparticles as active packaging for poultry products.

raw:
www.nature.com/scientificreports

Antimicrobial and biodegradable 
hydrogel based on nanocellulose/
alginate incorporated with silver 
nanoparticles as active packaging 
for poultry products

Noppon Somsesta1, Apichart Jinnapat1, Supachai Fakpiam1, Chanchai Suksanguan1, 
Varan Wongsan2, Wassikah Ouneam2, Supisara Wattanaeabpun2 & 
Intatch Hongrattanavichit2

In this research, active packaging which was made of all-natural component hydrogels from 
nanocellulose composited with silver nanoparticles at various concentrations (AgH) was studied. 
The concentration of silver nanoparticles ranged from 0.0078 to 0.0624 phr. AgH was characterized 
in terms of basic properties, functional properties, and packaging applications. Biocompatibility 
testing with the Caco-2 cell line showed that higher concentrations of silver (higher than 0.0312 phr) 
provided a lower cell viability rate (lower than 70% cell viability). Here, 0.0156 phr of silver nanoparticle 
concentration was the maximum loading that is safe for the target cell (82% cell viability) and was thus 
selected for use as active packaging. The antimicrobial activity showed that AgH at all concentrations 
inhibited both Gram bacteria up to 99.99%. Total volatile basic nitrogen compound testing showed 
that chicken meat preserved by AgH had the lowest values, indicating that AgH can prolong the shelf 
life in freshness level 1 (15% TVB-N) for 6.2 days compared to 3.9 and 4.1 days of blank and neat 
cellulose hydrogel. In addition, all AgH were gradually degraded over time and eventually disappeared 
within 15–30 days in organic soil.

Keywords  Hydrogel, Silver nanoparticles, Active packaging, Antimicrobial activity, TVB-N,  Poultry 
products

According  to  a  survey  conducted  by  the  UN  Environment  Programme  (UNEP),  the  global  volume  of  food 
waste was estimated at 931 million tonnes in 2019, amounting to approximately 17% of the total global food 
production1.  Food  loss  and  food  waste  lead  to  food  spoilage,  which  occurs  during  storage  and  preservation 
after slaughter. Generally, physical and chemical changes in food can generate unwanted substances, leading to 
microorganism contamination, which may cause adverse health effects. In poultry, chemical transformations also 
result in the formation of a group of amines, ammonia, and trimethylamine. These substances are responsible for 
the undesirable odor and color of food2.

One of the approaches to address the issue of food waste is to select suitable packaging or containers for specific 
food products, namely active packaging. The addition of particular materials to packages or active packaging 
enhances the product’s protection. When compared with conventional or passive packaging, active packaging 
not only extends the shelf life of the food product and improves its safety but also maintains the product quality. 
Active packaging can control and regulate the atmosphere within the package, which are achieved by employing 
several mechanisms (chemical, physical, and biological activities) that interact between the active packaging and 
the food product or the headspace above the food product3. Among numerous approaches, antimicrobial agents, 
such as sulfur compounds, organic acids, benzoates, and silver particles, are commonly used in active packaging 
technology to prevent food spoilage. Currently, there are mainly two groups of antimicrobial systems based on

Academy, Saraburi, Thailand. 2Department of Imaging and Printing Technology, Faculty of Science, Chulalongkorn 
University, Bangkok, Thailand. email: Intatch.h@chula.ac.th

Scientific Reports |        (2024) 14:27135 

| https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-78677-9

1

OPEN www.nature.com/scientificreports/

the migration of compounds: migrating or active release of specific substances in the atmosphere surrounding 
the product and nonmigrating, which is effective against microorganisms without intentional migration4.

Because  the  main  cause  of  reduced  food  shelf  life  and  food  spoilage  is  microbial  contamination,  various 
conventional processes, such as chemical disinfection, radiation, heat treatment, and precooking, are often used 
to overcome this issue. Unfortunately, these traditional techniques cannot be applied to all kinds of food, leading 
to many drawbacks. Innovative technologies, such as active packaging, have been proposed and developed to 
preserve and prolong food products while maintaining their quality and freshness. One of the most effective 
mechanisms that can prevent the contamination and growth of microorganisms, including bacteria and molds, 
is the release system. This system can reduce the quantity of bacteria present in the product by releasing the active 
substances from the packaging to the target. Active substances in the release system contribute to extending the 
product’s shelf life5. For example, Liu, et al.6 prepared a hydrogel from electrospinning nanofibers containing 
3-phenyllactic acid. The morphology of the hydrogel sample presented a highly porous structure, which affected 
the  3-phenyllactic  acid  release  rate.  The  sample  inhibited  the  growth  of  Staphylococcus  aureus  (S.  aureus) 
and  Escherichia  coli  (E.  coli)  and  was  compatible  with  Caco-2  and  SW480  cell  lines.  Castro-Mayorga,  et  al.7 
studied  biodegradable  active  packaging  comprising  poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate)  and  silver 
nanoparticles. The results showed that the composite sample which had only 0.040 wt% of silver nanoparticles 
inhibited the growth of Salmonella enterica and Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes) for at least 7 months. 
Marzlan, et al.8 reported the incorporation of essential oil from torch ginger [Etlingera elatior (Jack)] into an 
edible  starch-based  film.  The  film  was  applied  to  active  packaging  of  chicken  meat.  The  results  showed  that 
the film had high antioxidant property performance up to 84.78% ± 0.57%, which affected the rancidity of the 
fatty composition in chicken meat. The film also inhibited the growth of gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus, L. 
monocytogenes, and Bacillus subtilis) and gram-negative bacteria (Salmonella Typhi and E. coli) by presenting 
a  clear  zone  of  approximately  6.0 ± 0.01  to  23.0 ± 0.12  mm.  In  addition,  the  film  was  fully  biodegradable  in 
vegetable compost after 10 days.

Commercially, there is a high consumer demand for both fresh food with an extended shelf life and lower 
carbon  footprint  of  food  packaging.  Of  the  plastic  consumed,  approximately  80%  is  sent  to  landfills,  17%  is 
recycled  or  incinerated,  and  3%  ends  up  in  waterways.  However,  this  landfilling  method  results  in  pollution 
and  significant  land  resource  usage.  In  addition,  it  generates  odors  and  contributes  to  the  accumulation  of 
diseases9. Consequently, there is a demand for biodegradable polymers. The unsustainable use of crude oil as 
a feedstock to make traditional plastic provides a market for biopolymers to emerge into. In fact, the bioplastic 
market  is  forecast  to  grow  over  6  billion  USD  by  2023,  doubling  its  market  value  from  2018.  Interest  in  the 
food  packaging  and  distribution  industries  concerning  the  replacement  of  synthetic  polymers  has  also  been 
documented5. Therefore, biopolymers and biopolymer-based composites have received considerable attention 
from researchers over the past few decades. Along with their biodegradability, biopolymer-based composites 
also  possess  interesting  features,  such  as  renewability,  biocompatibility,  nontoxicity,  and  environmental 
friendliness. These natural materials exhibit great potential in different kinds of applications, such as medicals 
pharmaceuticals, textiles, cosmetics, and food. Biopolymers such as polylactic acid, starch, chitosan, and cellulose 
are  commonly  used  as  food  packaging  materials  because  of  their  biodegradable  and  barrier  properties  that 
protect food from the external environment10. However, the applications of biopolymers in their original form 
are limited because of their poor gas barrier, water sensitivity, and lower mechanical and thermal properties11. 
To overcome these challenges, various types of fillers, such as fibers, clays, carbon nanotubes, and graphene, are 
used  to  improve  these  properties.  Moreover,  advanced  and  innovative  technologies  have  been  introduced  to 
the food packaging industry due to the growing demand of customers for high quality, fresh, and healthy food. 
Recent research has demonstrated that biopolymer-based materials are very promising in advanced packaging 
technology. For example, Muthulakshmi, et al.12 produced a nanocellulose composited with silver nanoparticles 
that had antibacterial properties. Zhang, et al.13 studied a flexible adsorption material from cellulose and silver 
nanoparticles for postharvest packaging. This packaging promoted physical protection from compression force 
and  biological  protection  from  microorganisms.  Lei,  et  al.14  prepared  a  natural  hydrogel  based  on  cellulose 
nanofibers (CNFs) from corn stalk, pectin, chitosan, sodium alginate, and heteropolysaccharides. Lin, et al.15 
prepared  a  nanocellulose  hydrogel  using  a  metal  ion  crosslinker  and  reported  a  performance  comparison 
between a cellulose nanocrystal hydrogel and a CNF hydrogel.

In our research, we have discovered that one effective method to reduce food waste is to use active packaging, 
which  extends  the  shelf  life  of  food  and  ensures  the  safety  of  consumers,  promoting  a  better  quality  of  life 
and  well-being.  In  this  research,  natural  hydrogels  from  nanocellulose  and  alginate  incorporated  with  silver 
nanoparticles  (AgH)  at  various  concentrations  were  prepared.  The  AgH  were  characterized  in  terms  of 
chemical properties, morphology, crystallinity, thermal stability, mechanical properties, antimicrobial activity, 
cytotoxicity, and packaging applications. The hydrogels in this research were intended for use as meat exudate 
adsorbers, which are commonly found in fresh meat packaging.

Materials and methods
Materials
CNFs from coconut husk were prepared according to the CNF isolation method of Hongrattanavichit and Aht-
Ong16, in which coconut husk waste was supplied by a coconut farm at Prachuap Khiri Khan, Thailand. Briefly, 
the coconut husk was separated using a sieve with number 20 mesh (0.841-mm diameter) prior to treatment 
by a chemimechanical process. The chemicals used in the experiments of CNF preparation and CNF hydrogel 
preparation,  including  sodium  hydroxide  pellets,  hydrogen  peroxide,  calcium  chloride,  and  glycerol,  were 
purchased from CT Chemical (Bangkok, Thailand). Silver nanoparticles and sodium alginate were purchased 
from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). All purchased chemicals were of analytical reagent grade.

The toxicity of the CNF hydrogel composites at various silver nanoparticle concentrations was measured using 
the MTT assay. The Caco-2 cell line was chosen for this test because it is representative of a model of the human

cell line was selected for seeding in 48-well plates, in which each well contained 1.5 × 104 cells/200 µl. After 24 h 
of cultivation, the hydrogel samples were sterilized under UV rays for 2 h and added to the seeded wells. The 
seeded wells were incubated at 37 ℃ for 24 h. After that, each well was added with 200 µl of MTT solution and 
then incubated at 37 ℃ for 4 h under CO2 atmosphere. During incubation, yellow tetrazole in the MTT solution 
was transformed into purple formazan inside the living cells of the Caco-2 cell line. Then, a mixed solution of 
isopropanol and hydrochloric acid of approximately 200 µl was added to each well to dissolve purple formazan. 
Finally, the opacity density (OD) of purple formazan was measured at a wavelength of approximately 540 nm 
using a microplate reader. The percentage of cell viability of the Caco-2 cell line was calculated using Eq. (3).

Total volatile basic nitrogen compound (TVB-N) testing
The freshness of ground chicken during storage with the CNF hydrogel composited with silver nanoparticles 
at 0% and 0.0156% was measured via volatile nitrogen using TVB-N testing. Ground chicken was also stored 
without  the  CNF  hydrogel  composites  as  a  control.  Prior  to  testing,  fresh  and  clean  ground  chicken  was 
immediately purchased from a supermarket, which was produced daily at 8 a.m. Approximately 100 g of ground 
chicken was placed on the hydrogel which had 8.5 cm of diameter and 2 mm of thickness as presented in Fig. 1. 
During testing, the ground chicken was kept at 7 ℃ and sampled every 2 days. Distilled water of approximately 
25 ml was added to the chamber that contained 10 g of ground chicken, and they were blended for 30 min. The 
solution of the mixture was separated using a paper filter. The filtered solution was then used to measure the 
TVB-N content according to Liu, et al.6 and grade the degree of freshness according to the Chinese national 
standard GB 5009.228–2016.

Biodegradable properties
The biodegradability of the CNF hydrogel composites at various silver nanoparticle concentrations in organic soil 
was observed. Prior to observation, the samples were cut into rectangular shapes of approximately 1.5 × 1.5 cm. 
All hydrogels were placed into a paper tray, which had a diameter of approximately 3 cm, and then placed into 
the soil pit, which had diameter and depth of approximately 5 cm. Then, each soil pit was covered with organic 
soil. Water was sprayed once a day to provide soil moisture. The hydrogel samples were observed on days 0, 5, 
10, 15, and 30. The percentage of biodegradability was calculated using Eq. (4).

Statistical analysis
One-way analysis of variance was applied to the cytotoxicity, TVB-N, and biodegradability tests. Mean separation 
of data used the procedure of Duncan’s multiple range test with p < 0.05 significant difference.

Morphological properties
SEM  images  were  used  to  characterize  the  morphology  of  the  hydrogel  materials.  Figure  3  shows  the  cross 
section in nanoscale of the hydrogel samples at various silver nanoparticle concentrations. The figure shows that 
the cellulose fibers appear as dispersed nanofibers interwoven together in a mesh-like structure. In addition, 
the silver nanoparticles were distributed throughout the sample. However, at higher concentrations of 0.0312 
and 0.0624 phr, agglomeration of the silver nanoparticles was observed. In addition, the mapping images also 
show a dense group of dots that represented silver. This was because the high surface energy of nanoparticle 
materials, including silver nanoparticles, tends to minimize their surface energy by surface area reduction based 
on agglomeration12,18. Additionally, these agglomerates could introduce a number of flaws, which potentially 
have negative effects on the mechanical properties of the hydrogel.

Crystallinity index
X-ray  diffractogram  examination  was  used  to  investigate  the  crystallinity  and  the  incorporation  of  silver 
nanoparticles into the CNF hydrogel. Figure 4 shows the XRD patterns of the composite hydrogel at different 
silver  nanoparticle  concentrations.  The  composite  samples  displayed  broad  peaks  at  2θ  around  14°–16°  and 
22°–24°, which corresponded to the characteristic diffraction peaks of cellulose type I19. The diffraction peaks at 
2θ around 38°, 44°, 64°, and 77° were attributed to the XRD patterns of the silver nanoparticles, and the position 
of these peaks was in agreement with the study by Cabala and Acchar20. Moreover, the intensity of the diffraction 
pattern  increased  with  higher  concentrations  of  silver  in  the  composite;  therefore,  AgH0.0624  showed  the 
highest peaks because it contained the largest amount of silver. However, the addition of silver nanoparticles 
affected the crystallinity index. The percentage of crystallinity of the CNF hydrogel is listed in Table 1. Lower 
concentrations of silver nanoparticles decreased the percentage of crystallinity, whereas higher concentrations of 
silver nanoparticles enhanced the percentage of crystallinity. This may be because the presence of a small portion 
of fillers could disturb the crystal structure of the composite. In contrast, many fillers would act as nucleating 
agents within the hydrogel matrix, resulting in the enhancement of the recrystallization process21.

Thermal stability
TGA was used to determine the thermal behavior of the CNF hydrogel. The thermal properties of hydrogels 
referred to their thermal stability, as hydrogels were sensitive to temperature fluctuations that could impact their 
structure, integrity, and functionality. Furthermore, these properties were relevant to food packaging processes, 
e.g., retort process, which involved exposure to high temperature. The thermograms are shown in Fig. 5. The 
weight loss curves are divided into three steps. The initial step of mass loss below 100 ℃ corresponded to the 
evaporation of moisture on the surface and the adsorbed water within the composite. The next degradation step 
occurred in the temperature range from 200 to 300 ℃. This was related to the cleavage of glycosidic linkage, 
which  resulted  in  the  decomposition  of  alginate22.  The  last  major  weight  loss  was  observed  at  temperatures 
around 300–350 ℃ and was due to the thermal depolymerization of cellulose chains23. Interestingly, the thermal 
stability of cellulose gradually increased with increasing amount of silver nanoparticles. The degradation onset 
temperature of cellulose at different silver nanoparticle concentrations is reported in Table 1. This phenomenon 
was associated with the addition of particles to AgH. According to the crystallinity index of AgH, the addition 
of  silver  nanoparticles  increased  the  percentage  of  crystallinity  of  the  cellulose  hydrogel,  which  enhanced 
the thermal stability of the samples21. The char residue of AgH increased according to the silver nanoparticle 
concentration in the hydrogel.

Mechanical properties
The mechanical properties of the hydrogel samples were crucial factors for packaging applications, particularly in 
ensuring structural integrity, product protection, ease of handling, and consumer usability. The storage modulus 
(G′) and loss modulus (G″) of the hydrogel samples were measured in strain sweep mode (see Fig. 6 on left side). 
The G′ value indicates the stiffness of the gel material, while the G″ value reflects its viscous characteristics. The 
figure illustrates that G′ significantly surpasses G″, confirming that all samples exhibit hydrogel properties24.

Cytotoxicity testing
Biocompatibility testing using the MTT assay of the Caco-2 cell line was performed to indicate the toxicity of 
the  hydrogel  samples  at  various  silver  nanoparticle  concentrations.  The  Caco-2  cell  line  was  selected  in  this 
testing  because  this  cell  represents  intestinal  epithelial  cells  related  to  active  food  packaging.  Table  1  shows 
the  viability  of  cells  after  testing  with  the  hydrogel  samples.  Although  the  hydrogels  presented  antimicrobial 
properties,  the  AgH0  (100.00 ± 0.00),  AgH0.0078  (100.00 ± 0.00),  and  AgH0.0156  (82.00 ± 1.77)  samples  still 
had low cytotoxicity (high cell viability) after testing. However, the increase in silver nanoparticle concentration 
promoted more toxicity to the target cell line. According to the ISO 10993-5 standard, toxicity occurs when the 
cell survival rate is less than 70% 33. At concentrations of 0.0312 (AgH0.0312) and 0.0624 phr (AgH0.0624), the 
cell survival rates were 69.28 ± 3.84 and 68.62 ± 5.29, respectively,  indicating  that they were toxic to the cells 
because the cell viability was lower than 70%. This is because a high concentration of silver nanoparticles can 
impact or damage internal organs in humans6. Thus, AgH0.0156 that had a percentage of cell viability of more 
than 70% was chosen for the TVB-N test and further used on fresh chicken meat.

TVB-N testing
The amount of volatile nitrogen from ground chicken was analyzed using the TVB-N testing method. In this 
research, chicken meat was selected as a raw food material because of its high consumption in Thailand and 
across the world. Figure 7 shows the TVB-N value of ground chicken stored with AgH0 and AgH0.0156 and 
without a hydrogel (as a control) at 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 days. As the storage time increases, the TVB-N value of all 
samples increases, especially the AgH0 and control samples. This is because chicken meat in nature undergoes 
spoilage with the release of nitrogen gas, leading to chemical and physical changes. This affected the biological 
and biogenic amine substances, which were the results of three processes: decarboxylation, reductive amination, 
and transamination of aldehydes and ketones. During the spoilage of chicken meat, there was an increase in 
the  amount  of  protein  or  components  that  contained  nitrogen  gas  from  bacteria.  This  resulted  in  increased 
proteolysis  and  autolysis,  leading  to  the  release  of  amino  acids.  The  presence  of  amino  acids  and  bacteria 
indicates  the  ability  to  induce  the  decarboxylation  process,  which  further  accelerated  spoilage  and  resulted 
in  the  production  of  metabolites  and  increased  biogenic  amines2.  However,  AgH0.0156  consistently  had  the 
lowest TVB-N value on each sampling day. This was because the hydrogel with added silver nanoparticles had a 
mechanism that inhibited bacterial growth.

According to the Chinese national standard GB 5009.228–2016, freshness level 1 corresponds to the TVB-N 
value  in  the  range  of  0–15  mg/100  g.  The  chicken  meat  of  freshness  level  1  presented  a  suitable  quality  for 
consumption because it was safe and had good firmness of meat texture, good appearance in terms of color, high 
nutrition, no odor, and good taste. In addition, the standard also specified that freshness level 2 corresponds to 
the TVB-N value exceeding 25 mg/100 g6. Considering freshness level 1, when the TVB-N value was less than or 
equal to 15 mg/100 g, the control sample had an approximate shelf life of 3.9 days, the CNF hydrogel sample had 
a shelf life of approximately 4.1 days, and the AgH sample had the longest shelf life at 6.2 days. On day 10, the 
control sample started to show signs of spoilage; as the TVB-N value exceeded 25 mg/100 g, the AgH0 sample

Biodegradable properties
Because  of  environmental  awareness,  sustainable  or  biodegradable  materials  are  anticipated  to  expand  and 
grow  annually  in  the  food  packaging  industry.  Biodegradation  will  be  considered  an  additional  requirement 
in packaging technology in the upcoming years. The biodegradability of the hydrogel samples was evaluated in 
terms of physical changes in the specimens and percentage of weight reduction, as shown in Fig. 6 on right side. 
Regarding physical appearance, the alterations in the hydrogel samples were clearly noticeable. The degradation 
of the samples occurred progressively over the span of 15 days, with further decomposition observed between 
days 15 and 30, as shown in the tiny photograph in Fig. 6 on right side.

According to the weight loss of the hydrogel, the initial stage of biodegradation started on day 5 with a drastic 
decrease of over 80%. After that, all hydrogels gradually degraded over time and eventually disappeared on days 
15–30. Moreover, the obtained data showed greater biodegradable properties or less decay time compared to 
those based on nanocellulose/alginate in other works34,35. According to ASTM 6400 and EN13432, a material is 
considered biodegradable when at least 90% of its mass is decomposed under the action of microorganisms within 
180 days. Therefore, the experimental results indicate that all hydrogel samples possess good biodegradability 
and are potential alternatives to petroleum-based plastics.

Conclusion
This  research  investigated  the  preparation  and  characterization  of  hydrogels  based  on  cellulose/alginate 
incorporated  with  silver  nanoparticles  at  varying  concentrations  (0,  0.0078,  0.0156,  0.0312,  and  0.0624  phr). 
FESEM images elucidated the three-dimensional structure of cellulose fibers at the nanoscale with distributed 
silver  nanoparticles,  confirming  the  efficacy  of  hydrogel  synthesis.  The  findings  underscored  that  increased 
concentrations of silver nanoparticles correlated with improved crystallinity index and enhanced thermal stability 
of the hydrogel samples. However, the augmented presence of active particles adversely affected the mechanical 
properties and cytotoxicity of the hydrogel samples. Notably, all hydrogels demonstrated remarkable efficacy in 
inhibiting both Gram bacteria at a rate of 99.99% and extended the freshness (level 1) of poultry products to 6.2 
days, surpassing the comparative duration of 3.9 days. Furthermore, the biodegradation study revealed that the 
integrated hydrogels decomposed in organic soil within 30 days, exhibiting negligible disparity compared to the 
neat hydrogel. The integration of the cellulose-based hydrogel with silver nanoparticles demonstrated promising 
potential for fabricating active packaging solutions capable of both exudate absorption and controlled release of 
antimicrobial agents. This advancement has significant implications for enhancing food safety, prolonging shelf 
life, and fostering environmental sustainability.
